RE: Letter of Support for LD 560 - Bond Issue for Coastal Climate Resiliency
Dear Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and Distinguished Committee Members,
As the Emergency Management Director for York County, I am writing to express my strong support for LD 560, "An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Improve Coastal Climate Resiliency." This $75 million bond issue represents a critical and timely investment in the future safety and economic stability of Maine's coastal communities.
The urgency of this legislation has been underscored by the recent announcement that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is no longer funding certain mitigation programs. This decision signals that Maine must take responsibility for its own resilience planning and implementation.
York County has recently experienced the devastating impacts of extreme weather, including the damage from the federally declared disaster in January 2024 (DR-4764) that caused extensive destruction along our coast. Our coastal dunes and beaches were destroyed, and our coastline has been left vulnerable and exposed to the next storm. This is underscored by the fact that our communities are managing challenges such as:
� Significant damage to public infrastructure and private property from recent storm events; in York County alone, we saw over $40M in municipal damages, over $1.15M in federal aid go to individuals who experience property damage and loss, and several million dollars' worth of damage to local beaches and dunes from the January 2024 disaster
� Storm surge impacts threatening critical facilities in our coastal towns � Key evacuation routes vulnerable to inundation � Beach erosion threatening both public access and the tourism economy that supports tens of
thousands of local jobs and over $1.6B in annual spending
The proposed bond issue offers Maine an opportunity to demonstrate self-sufficiency. By investing in municipal, county, and regional resilience projects, we can proactively protect our infrastructure, natural resources, and communities from hazards we've already experienced. This approach is not only more

cost-effective than responding to disasters after they occur but also ensures the continuity of essential services and protection of our coastal communities.
As emergency management professionals, we know that every dollar invested in disaster mitigation saves approximately six dollars in future disaster costs. The investments we can make due to the $75 million bond issue will not only create immediate jobs and economic activity but will prevent hundreds of millions in potential damages across our coastal regions in the years to come.
It is imperative that Maine establish its own funding mechanisms for coastal preparedness and hazard mitigation measures. As such, I urge the committee to support LD 560 and recommend its passage to the full legislature.
Thank you for your consideration. I am available to provide additional information or answer any questions the committee may have.
Sincerely,
Arthur W. Cleaves Director York County Emergency Management Agency Email: awcleaves@yorkcountymaine.gov

Testimony of Mayor of the City of Portland, Mark Dion
Before Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee
In Support of LD 560, An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Improve Coastal Climate
Resiliency
April 9, 2025
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and Honorable Members of the Committee, I write on behalf of the City of Portland in strong support of LD 560, which proposes a $75 million general fund bond issue to improve coastal climate resiliency and support the long-term sustainability of Maine's shoreline communities.
As a coastal city, Portland is acutely aware of the growing risks associated with sea level rise, increased storm surges, and changing weather patterns. These impacts pose significant threats to public infrastructure, housing, economic activity, and public safety in our working waterfront and surrounding neighborhoods. The scale of investment needed to prepare for these challenges far exceeds what individual municipalities can fund on their own.
LD 560 recognizes the urgent need for state-level support by establishing a grant program for municipal, county, tribal, and regional governments to undertake meaningful resilience planning and engineering upgrades. This funding would enable communities like Portland to reinforce critical infrastructure, adapt our waterfront assets, and proactively address vulnerabilities through both built and natural mitigation strategies.
These investments not only protect lives and property but also ensure that Maine's coastal economy, which contributes substantially to the state's GDP, remains strong and viable into the future. For cities like Portland, where the waterfront is a hub for commerce, tourism, marine trades, and transportation, climate resiliency is both an environmental and economic imperative.

April 7, 2024 To: The Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Committee Members: I am writing in empathic support of LD560, An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Improve Coastal Climate Resiliency. There is really no other way to state this other than that without this funding many of the State's beaches may not survive. We cannot put a timetable on this potential apocalypse as storm seasons luctuate, but after 2024 some sandy shorelines are on the brink of disappearing. There are three potential ways to attack the problem: mitigate, adapt, or do nothing. Doing nothing is clearly the most expensive option. Everyone loses. Adaptation can be effective but in many cases it becomes a race against time. You can maybe build higher or retreat if there is room, but eventually the rising tide will catch up. Mitigation allows us to ight the symptoms and take an offensive stance. This bond will fund mitigation efforts that are desperately needed. As Vice President of the nonpro it Save our Shore Saco Bay (SOS), we are currently working with the York County Emergency Management team to build engineered beaches designed to withstand 100-year storms. This will provide FEMA relief for sand and dune loss from any declared disaster and lessen damage from those that do not reach that quali ication. This effort is dif icult and expensive. Funding from this bond will go a long way to help make it a reality. If we give up on beaches, we face the consequences of billions of dollars lost from Maine's biggest industry - tourism. This funding is well worth the return on investment. I, and the membership of SOS, urge you to lead the way to preserve, and enable growth, of our greatest natural resource. Thank you
David Plavin Vice President, Save Our Shores Saco Bay Saco, Maine

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs, my name is Dorma Bailey, and I proudly represent Senate District 31, which includes Buxton, Old Orchard Beach, and Saco. Today I am pleased to introduce my bill LD 560, "An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to
Improve Coastal Climate Resiliency."
During my time in the Maine House and Senate, I have long been committed to addressing
coastal issues and finding ways to protect our communities from the impacts of strong, coastal
storms. I am sure that many of us recall the severe winter storms of 2023 and 2024 that wrecked
Maine's coastline, damaging businesses and homes, flooding our streets, and hurting our working waterfronts.
Earlier this session, I offered testimony in support of 1, "An Act to Increase Storm
Preparedness for Maine's Communities, Homes, and Infrastructure." As I said then, I did
not hesitate to support the Governor's and the Legislature's proposal to allocate a historic $60
million in financial assistance and relief. It was the largest -- and very necessary ~ investment in
storm relief in Maine's history. Unfortunately, due to the increasingly severe effects of climate change, it camiot be the last. The storms will continue to form and grow, and they will continue to inflict damage on our beautiful state - and all those who live, study, work, travel or retire here
At that public hearing, I introduced an amendment to highlight the role of county governments. York County has taken a lead, coordinating role to improve beach resilience across the region to
upgrade beaches and dunes to FEMA Category G. It's a higher classification that FEMA will
help rebuild to -- but only if we upgrade before the storm.
Also, York County worked on allocating ARPA funding for the dredge that helps manage
erosion of ports and rivers in the area. In the spirit of the Community Resilience Partnership and various Council of Governments, we know that it's highly cost-effective, efficient, and practical to collaborate and coordinate - rather than leave individual smaller municipalities to fend for
themselves.
1

For these reasons, I also recently signed a letter of support for the York County Emergency Management Agency to seek funding for its York County Coastal Sand Dune Restoration and Protection Initiative. If funded, this project would support the restoration of dunes and beaches
for two municipalities in my district -- Old Orchard Beach and Saco - to FEMA Category G
standards. By fimding the engineering costs and subsequent construction, we can help
municipalities restore critical coastal defenses and provide long-term hazard mitigation benefits for businesses, residents, and visitors alike.

I share these examples because it's critical that we recognize the good work being done, as well

as the additional funding, planning, and work that must take place in order to restore, strengthen,

and preserve Maine's beaches, coasts, and dunes.

'

LD 5 60 would issue a bond in the amount of $75,000,000 for county, municipal, and tribal
govermnents, as well as regional councils, to apply for grants. These grants would improve coastal climate resiliency and upgrade engineered beaches along Maine's 228 miles of coastline, including in the communities of Old Orchard Beach and Saco.

From raging floodwaters to rising storm surges, we are not fully protected from the increasingly damaging and severe effects of climate change in Maine. Whether it's Camp Ellis, the Hook on Chebeague Island, or Popham Beach, coastal communities are in crisis. With this bond, we can
provide Mainers the opportunity to choose to continue historic investments in climate resilience.
In this way, we can ensure that the Maine we all know and love will be here for generations to
come.

Thank you for your time. I would be happy to answer any questions.

LD 560 Bond support: As President of SOS Saco Bay, I am in full support of the proposed $75m bond for Coastal Resiliency. I want to take a different angle from prior coastal resiliency effort support and be specific of where proceeds can be used that create Made in Maine manufacturing activity with needed coastal infrastructure. Our group follows Living Shorelines Solutions, a Gulf Coast installer/designer of Wave Attenuation Devices (WADs), pyramid shaped concrete structures installed to protect shoreline/infrastructure from hurricane force storms. These WADs are now protecting the famous Skyway Bridge in Tampa Bay, allowing sand to come through with incoming tides/storms but harder for sand to recede out from the shore. We envision these WAD's to similarly protect Maine beaches and infrastructure, one model project could be Ferry Beach State Park in Saco for sand gain/acretion. And regardless of location, these WAD solutions need to be manufactured locally at suitable harbors (with related infrastructure support for water transfer). A win/win for jobs and the environment.

Testimony of Rep. Lori K. Gramlich in support of
LD 560, An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Improve
Coastal Climate Resiliency
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and honorable members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, I am Lori Gramlich. I have the honor of representing House District 131, which is the lovely seaside community of Old Orchard Beach, and of serving as Assistant House
Majority Leader. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today as the lead cosponsor in support of LD
560, An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Improve Coastal Climate Resiliency.

Beach erosion has devastating impacts, not only on our enviromnent but also on our coastal economy. That's especially true in connnunities like mine, where our beaches are the comerstone of our local economy and also serve as a protective buffer between us and the incredible might of the waters of the Gulf of Maine. In light of sea-level rise and extreme weather events, these precious resources have
sustained serious damage and continue to face grave threats.

Throughout my time in the Legislature, I have worked on initiatives to protect our beaches and coastline.
In fact, the very first bill I submitted as a newly elected first--term legislator was to protect our beaches
and sand dunes, and I have continued my focus in this policy area, including during my time as House chair of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee. I am proud of the work we have done and
continue to do in this arena, but I also know that we must do more in light of the gravity of our situation.

A prime example of the threat our beaches and coastline are facing is the damage my community of Old

Orchard Beach sustained in January of 2024. Back-to-back winter storms caused unprecedented

flooding and damage to residences, businesses and infrastructure. In some cases, people lost the entire

first floors of their homes. Roads were closed for weeks or months. The impact of these storms was

nothing short of devastating to Old Orchard Beach, specifically Ocean Park, which was hit particularly

hard but was by no means the only community in Maine to face such staggering damage. _

V

District 131: Old Orchard Beach

The reality of global climate change and the extreme weather events it causes can often seem like a far~ off problem - a problem for other states, perhaps California or Florida, to grapple with. January 2024 made it clear that climate change is not a distant threat; indeed, it is knocking at our door. More than a year later, Old Orchard Beach residents and other coastal Mainers are still recovering from
the effects of 2024's extreme winter storms. We cannot change the past, but we can recognize that these events foreshadow future extreme weather. We absolutely cannot afford to be unprepared. With roughly
3,500 miles of coastline, Maine and its residents are uniquely vulnerable to future extreme weather events along our shores. The cost of preparedness pales in comparison to the price tag of responding
after the fact.
LD 560 is one key to ensuring we are ready. It would send a $75 million bond issue out to Maine voters
for approval, and if approved, the funds would be used to award grants to regional, county, municipal and Tribal entities to support climate resilience efforts along our coastline. I would like to take a
moment to emphasize the importance of including counties here. Maine's county-level emergency management agencies play such an important role in disaster preparedness, response, mitigation and recovery -- something I have seen firsthand and deeply appreciated in York County.
Last winter, it was my community and a number of other coastal towns that faced devastation. But let me be clear: Any of our many, many coastal communities could be next. Let's make sure we have done
all we can to prepare and protect the property and indeed the safety of the Mainers who live in those
communities.
Thank you for your consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have for me.
District 131: Old Orchard Beach
